title: The AI Steering Tax in L&D
author: Philippa Hardman
summary: After a month observing ~100 L&D professionals across two professional-services firms, logging every prompt, output, and decision, Hardman reports that people want AI that challenges them, not AI that does the work for them, and that what they want changes at every stage of the workflow. Her central concept is the "AI Steering Tax": the time, energy, and skill users must spend to push AI from its agreeable, shallow default toward genuinely useful output, a price most professionals cannot afford, so they settle for the fluent first pass. She argues sycophancy, confidence inflation, and reflection-without-origination are documented product defects to engineer out, not user problems, while the market keeps selling a faster production line to people who are asking for a judgement partner.
points: Across two firms, the most-valued AI moments were never finished work but moments where AI pushed thinking, sparred, interrogated a weak brief, or pressure-tested a recommendation.
Challenge must not become gatekeeping: users liked a "pair designer" that offered counterarguments but hated a "process enforcer" that blocked their momentum.
What people want from AI shifts by stage, argue with me at diagnosis, generate with me at design, discipline me at evaluation, with the biggest unmet needs at diagnosis and evaluation.
The "AI Steering Tax" is what users pay to move AI from its default agreeable behaviour to the behaviour they actually need; most cannot afford it, so they settle for the shallow first pass.

Sycophancy, confidence inflation, and reflection-without-origination are documented, structural product defects to design out, yet the ~$2.2bn L&D AI market sells production tools to people who want a judgement partner.
quotes: People who design & develop learning in the workplace want AI that challenges them, not AI that does the work for them
The moments people rated most were the ones where AI pushed their thinking — sparring on ideas, interrogating a weak brief, pressure-testing a recommendation.

The cost of that pushing — the multiple questions, the re-runs, the stripping of your own framing — is what I call the AI Steering Tax: what users pay to move AI from its default behaviour to the behaviour they actually need.
Sycophancy, confidence inflation and reflection-without-origination are product defects, not user problems — documented, structural, and designable-out.
The market is inverted: a production-line industry serving a judgement-partner demand. Whoever builds for the demand side first owns the category.
the doer opportunity is being widely exploited; the thought partner opportunity is wide open.
